speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs what regulatory requirements and policy measures are in place to prevent risks arising from crowd surges during festive periods and at public events.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs whether there are adequate crowd control measures whenever there are large-scale events involving large numbers of members of the public so as to avoid crowd crushes or stampedes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) what lessons are learnt from the recent stampede incidents in several countries; (b) whether further enhancements to our crowd control measures by the relevant agencies will be needed; and (c) if needed, what are these.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs what strategies are put in place to proactively manage crowds at large scale public and private events and ensure that they do not develop into crowd pushing, crushing and collapses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) whether the Ministry has identified a list of locations or events in Singapore at risk of crowd surge and stampede situations; (b) what are some of these locations or events; and (c) what are the enhanced safety steps that organisers at these locations or events are required to put in place.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) whether SPF proactively informs the public of crowd surge risks and ways to stay safe when participating in large public events; and (b) whether tear gas will ever be used in crowded, confined spaces for the purpose of crowd control.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) whether Singapore has an occupant load limit for large assembly points; and (b) how is this limit monitored during events with large crowds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) works with the relevant stakeholders to put in place measures to mitigate the risks associated with large crowds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police will, then, engage these EOs on the appropriate measures to be deployed for public safety.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These plans may include measures such as the monitoring of crowd size, the deployment of security personnel and the regulation of crowd flow at congregation areas and potential chokepoints.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They may also include cordoning off areas with public safety risks, such as narrow pathways and bridges and signages to guide the public on diversions and closures of thoroughfares.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police are deployed on-the-ground at these major events to ensure law and order, as well as to provide swift responses to incidents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These may involve catering for emergency lanes to facilitate emergency responses within crowded areas and closing off high-risk areas pre-emptively before they become overcrowded.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As for indoor venues, occupant limits are regulated by the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) under the Fire Code and Fire Safety Manager (FSM) Regulations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Under the Fire Code, functional spaces within a building are assigned an occupant load factor which determines the maximum number of people allowed at any point of time and there must also be sufficient egress capacity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In general, the Fire Code requires every storey of a building to have at least two independent exit staircases to ensure timely evacuation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police conduct frequent patrols when there are large crowds at locations like Little India and Chinatown, and also deploy various sensors, such as CCTVs and drones to monitor the ground situation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They may be augmented by Auxiliary Police Officers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members of the public may call 999 to alert the Police if there are safety concerns related to overcrowding.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the Police assesses that there are disturbances to the mood of a crowd, the Police may seek to remove the source of the agitation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police may also provide adequate space for crowd dispersal or provide clear instructions on how the crowd may exit the congested area.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To do so, the Police may use voice amplification devices, such as loudhailers, to gain the attention of the crowd.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To increase public awareness, the Police publicise safety measures pre-, during and post-event.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police may also pre-empt the public on potential crowding and alert the public to avoid areas or events which are already crowded.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members of the public can help keep each other safe by informing one another of ground developments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Police regularly analyse major incidents, which occur around the world to improve their crowd management measures.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They also regularly review their regulatory and policy levers, as well as operational plans.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is equally important that organisers and stakeholders act responsibly, including to adopt sufficient safety measures and to work with the authorities to keep events and the public safe.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What lessons has MHA learnt or drawn from the recent tragedies in South Korea and Indonesia, to ensure that such incidents do not occur in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand as the Minister of State said that MHA does read and understand what happens in other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, will the Ministry be obtaining and studying the detailed investigation reports from the respective governments?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First and foremost, many of the questions filed were about the number of persons or the size of the crowd.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But I think what is also important to understand and acknowledge is that it is not just about the absolute size of the crowd.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: You can have a situation whereby the absolute size is not very large, but actually, they are in a very concentrated, very congested area; and that there might not be entry and exit points that are regularly available.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, I just wanted to clarify and elaborate that it is not just about the absolute size of the crowd, but about the specific terrain that we are looking at.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Just based on recent memory, I do not think there have been recent incidents whereby we use tear gas because we acknowledge that it can cause public chaos.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, another lesson that we have learnt from looking at incidents that happen overseas is that the actions that we take have to be proportionate and we have to be very careful in the way we handle such incidents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have Clementi residents who saw what happened at these tragedies elsewhere in the world and were concerned as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The first question is, do our agencies look for situations where there may be multiple events, multiple gatherings that individually do not cross the threshold for notification but which may actually lead to a substantial crowd, either by coincidence or by just the organic growth of the crowd around these events and gatherings?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I say this because I have had Clementi residents who were able to attend F1 this year and they felt that the crowds were quite substantial after the race ended and when people were heading home, heading off in multiple different directions through different thoroughfares.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Tan, do keep your supplementary questions shorter, please.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: One is that it typically happens around specific festivals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Because the Police would already be quite well aware that this particular venue is a place where crowds typically can gather and they will gather around specific times of the year; and they would be on standby, there would be Police patrols to ensure that there is law and order and to disperse crowds if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the second point, indeed, I had mentioned in my earlier reply, about both entries and exits, and is not just about physical doors.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is also about how people move in and out of an event.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Many of us would have attended National Day Parades and all sorts of other large-scale events before.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: You would have noticed that we have road diversions and we have had crowd marshals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That will take place both before and after an event.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the hon Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I wonder whether the Police is minded to develop bespoke regulations to deal with different types of crowds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, a crowd at a rock concert would behave differently from a crowd at a place of worship.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is something that is found in scientific literature and the practical considerations are different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I wonder whether the Police could consider this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, on the point about voice amplification made by the hon Minister of State, I wonder whether the Police is minded to leverage on technology.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, issuing SMS text messages at a particular area so that all the people in the crowd would get the right message and act in accordance with the Police advice.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It always allows us to further think about how we can improve our processes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Indeed, we also do pay attention to the dynamics of the crowd – what kind of people are likely to attend, what kind of fervour or enthusiasm or emotions they will likely display.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When the Police work with the EOs in the first instance to think about how to best manage the crowd.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the second point, definitely, we are always on the lookout for better use of technology.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I would have to check internally whether or not we use it to send out SMS notifications, but that is one possibility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I just want to ask whether  MHA has identified some areas where it would advise the public not to hold events that could lead to these possible consequences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Yes, like I mentioned earlier, we work very actively with EOs in the first instance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, when we are aware that EOs want to specifically organise an event, and at that point in time, when they submit their application, they would already mention the venue, the likely crowd size and what their crowd control measures are.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: At that point in time, if the venue is not something that is suitable, the Police would already inform them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, at Clarke Quay and Boat Quay, where many pubs organise New Year Countdown events.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Who would the Police typically liaise with, in trying to manage the crowd, where there are large crowds of people in those areas?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, Clarke Quay and Boat Quay, where there are New Year Countdowns.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Like my earlier response, I believe it was to Dr Tan Wu Meng, we are aware that there are certain venues that typically over festivities, there would be crowds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Sometimes, they may also activate volunteers – some of the EOs may have volunteers – to take into account what the overall crowd management situation should be like.
